column3: Parallel kalla/bal reversal: denial of the deferred Judgment explains the present attachment.
Knowledge of all things does not specifically clarify love of the immediate.
Forbids rushing reception, directly framing haste as interference with an ordered process.
Parallel kalla/bal identifies failure to fear the Hereafter as the corrective contrast.
The radiant face of that Day supplies the deferred horizon opposed to the immediate.
Direct parallel: loving the immediate is paired with leaving a weighty Day behind.
Parallel reversal links present moral neglect with the critique of immediate priorities.
Looking toward its Lord develops the deferred orientation of the adjacent passage.
Grain imagery alone does not establish the temporal preference in 75:20.
What people earn seals their hearts, supporting an inwardly formed preference.
The early summons only loosely echoes the channel of hurried, available provision.
Intense love of worldly good shows attachment as a forceful, binding disposition.
Wanting the immediate and its partial grant expose the limits of controlling outcomes by haste.
Explanation belongs to the ordered sequence, countering a demand for premature possession.
Hidden and public conduct is known, but the verse only indirectly concerns inward preference.

The mustard seed is not evidence for a temporal or affective preference.
Giving what one loves tests whether attachment can be redirected beyond immediate possession.
Gathering and recitation are assigned before response, establishing a non-hurried order.
A near victory may be loved without becoming the ultimate priority, preserving a secondary reading.
Love is made answerable to following, not treated as self-validating attachment.

Desire for forgiveness can redirect attachment toward pardon and generous action.

Wanting worldly gain versus the Hereafter displays competing orientations within one crisis.
The greater punishment of the Hereafter supplies only a broad deferred contrast.

The self-satisfied turn away after refusal depicts conduct consistent with the passage’s preference.
Jealous attachment shows how love can make a present, scarce good govern judgment.
Hastening punishment is shown as defiant impatience, not mastery of its appointed time.
The question about entering Saqar adds little beyond the deferred consequence.
Haste is presented as a deep human tendency that must not govern reception of signs.
Going ahead is questioned because it disrupts responsibility to those left behind.
The oath by Resurrection fixes the passage’s deferred frame for judging present preference.
Loving the spread of indecency shows desire functioning as a durable motive with consequences.
A gathered, excessive love of wealth closely parallels attachment to what is presently at hand.
Impatient calling from outside the chambers illustrates failure to respect proper timing and order.
The verse’s love concerns disciplined ranks, not immediate versus deferred preference.
Kalla redirects confidence in accumulated wealth toward an unavoidable destructive outcome.
Human formation from a drop supports a measured developmental sequence rather than instant completion.
Refusing attachment to a setting object distinguishes enduring commitment from transient appearance.
Preferring worldly life is a close parallel formulation of choosing the near over the lasting.
The nighttime ruin only loosely supports the channel’s concern with available provision and timing.
Divine non-love of deniers does not directly explain attachment to the immediate.

Resurrection confirms that present preference is evaluated against a real future restoration.
Seed-splitting offers a distant maturation image, useful only as auxiliary evidence.
Kalla and future knowing oppose present heedlessness with deferred disclosure.
The resurrection question adds only an indirect future horizon.
Hastening punishment ignores that its arrival can overtake ordinary time without warning.
Kalla denies any refuge, making immediate security inadequate before the coming reality.
The denial of further punishment exemplifies rejecting accountability beyond the first death.
The ban on excess may limit consumption, but it does not specifically address temporal love.
Kalla with future knowing makes eventual disclosure the answer to present dispute.
Bliss for the righteous provides only a general opposite future outcome.
Withholding immediate evil preserves a term and exposes the limits of human haste.
Kalla identifies the blaze as the reality that overturns present escape assumptions.
Human diversity and piety do not specifically clarify love of the immediate.
Love of the equitable is not a temporal preference and remains only a broad contrast.
The repeated future knowing intensifies the deferred correction to present ignorance.
The facial response has only a remote channel link to premature judgment.
The rule against transgression does not add to the temporal preference at issue.
Not yet completing the command supports the distinction between an unfinished process and closure.
The exception for companions of the right adds no clear temporal or affective evidence.
Preferring worldly life over the Hereafter is a direct conceptual parallel to 75:20.
Speech is recorded and punishment extended, shifting confidence from the present to reckoning.
The failure of intercession does not specifically illuminate immediate love.
Demanding one’s share before the Day of account directly portrays premature claim on judgment.
Human createdness offers at most a broad corrective to present presumption.
The statement about not being guardians does not address the focus’s temporal preference.
It can contrast apparent numerical gain with real increase, but only indirectly.
Stubborn resistance to signs does not itself explain attachment to the immediate.
The drink of those brought near offers only a distant positive future contrast.
Hidden seeds and exhaustive knowledge lightly support inwardness, not immediate preference itself.
Kalla rejects panicked present calculation and directs trust toward forthcoming guidance.
Wanting individually unrolled sheets depicts a demand for immediate, personalized delivery.
Competing loves show that attachment can misplace ultimate allegiance, though not specifically its timing.
Future repudiation reverses a present attachment, exposing its eventual instability.
Claimed divine belovedness is corrected by accountable human condition, testing love claims.
Hope before entering the Garden supplies only a limited deferred orientation.
What people love may be harmful, so immediate attraction cannot settle what is truly good.
Kalla rejects immediate fear and sends the messengers forward under promised accompaniment.
Mutual love is shown in durable moral qualities, contrasting with a merely acquisitive attachment.
Present submission on that Day supplies the ultimate reversal of current resistance.
Hastening evil before good directly figures an attempt to pull consequence ahead of its time.

Do not hasten the Quran before its revelation is completed, directly paralleling ordered reception.
Love of good is expressed through generosity and restraint, offering a contrary formed disposition.
Patience and refusal to hasten leave the promised event to its proper time.
The general call to obey adds no specific evidence about immediate love.
Correction of a claim about divine giving and non-love of corrupters is only broadly relevant.
A named term explains delayed punishment as appointment, not uncertainty or loss of control.
The messenger-witness pattern supplies only a general warning and future accountability.
Attraction to desired worldly goods gives a direct inventory of the near objects that can govern love.

The request for a short reprieve foregrounds attachment to a brief present term.
Seeking the transient gain of worldly life directly warns against acting for immediate acquisition.
Wanting worldly reward is contrasted with the availability of both worldly and final reward.
Being satisfied with worldly life in place of the Hereafter is a direct counterpart to 75:20.
A counted postponement of punishment establishes delay as an appointed measure, not absence.
Those who want worldly life and its adornment receive their present return within its limits.
Worldly enjoyment is explicitly set as slight in relation to the Hereafter.
The plea for a short delay exposes recognition of a missed future-oriented opportunity.
The coming command is not to be hastened, directly rejecting demands to advance its time.
Seizure is deferred to an appointed term, making postponement part of measured judgment.
Human beings pray for harm as for good and are characterized by haste.

Following present adornment and desire is opposed to patient orientation with remembrance.

A fixed appointment governs punishment even when immediate seizure is possible.
Those astray are left extended until they see the promised consequence, preserving deferred disclosure.
Musa's hastening toward his Lord supplies a contrary case in which haste has a distinct object and setting.
The demand for the promise to arrive is a direct form of impatient challenge.
Seeking punishment early is answered by divine time, for which a day has a different measure.

Denial of the Hour is paired with the prepared blaze, clarifying the suppressed deferred reality.
Demanding immediate angelic encounter or vision illustrates a demand for premature confirmation.
The objection that the Quran was not delivered all at once closely parallels resistance to staged completion.
Hastening evil before good repeats the inversion of proper temporal order.
The possibility that part of what is hastened may already be close weakens confidence in controlling its arrival.
Worldly provision is temporary adornment; what is with God is better and more lasting.
Seeking the final abode while not forgetting one's worldly share preserves a non-rejecting hierarchy of goods.
Worldly life is characterized as diversion and play in contrast to the real final life.
Knowing the outward of worldly life while heedless of the Hereafter describes the narrowed horizon behind 75:20.
The warning against worldly deception guards against present life displacing the coming Day.
Choosing worldly life and adornment is set against a different prophetic household orientation.
The Hour may be near despite uncertainty, challenging assumptions that the deferred is remote.
The appointed Day cannot be delayed or advanced, directly denying human control of its timing.
Worldly life must not deceive, making present attraction an unreliable guide.
The demand for the promise repeats the impatient interrogation of deferred accountability.
Worldly life is passing enjoyment and the Hereafter the abiding home.
Those without faith seek to hasten the Hour, while believers regard it as true.
The desired harvest of the Hereafter and the desired harvest of the world form an explicit competing orientation.
The Hour comes suddenly while people are unaware, overturning ordinary present calculation.

Worldly life is described as temporary play, adornment, rivalry, and accumulation, then set against the Hereafter.
Looking to what one has sent ahead supplies a practical contrary orientation to immediate attachment.
Wealth and children can distract from remembrance, identifying present possessions as competing claims.
Wealth and children are a test, qualifying attachment to immediate goods.

What was sent ahead and left behind makes present action answerable to a later disclosure.
The self bears insight against itself, supporting the inward source of the passage's preference.
The bleak face on that Day extends the adverse future outcome within the immediate context.
The arrival at the collarbone depicts the limit at which immediate life can no longer be retained.

Transgression is paired with preferring worldly life, forming a direct conceptual parallel.
Preferring worldly life is given its final consequence, clarifying the stakes of 75:20.
Fearing the final standing and restraining desire supplies the contrary inner discipline.
The Garden as refuge completes the contrary future-directed orientation.
The Hereafter is explicitly better and more enduring than the worldly life preferred in the preceding verse.
Failure to urge feeding the poor shows the social cost of a self-enclosed present orientation.
Devouring inheritance greedily specifies acquisitive conduct alongside excessive love of wealth.
The overturning of graves makes the buried future judgment the answer to present attachment.
What is in breasts is brought out, directly connecting final disclosure to inward attachments.
Competition for more distracts until the graves, closely describing present acquisitiveness displacing the end.
Arrival at the graves marks the boundary that exposes the short reach of accumulation.
Future seeing of the Blaze counters the present distraction of rivalry and increase.
Certainty of that later seeing intensifies the deferred corrective.
Questioning about blessing turns present enjoyment into later accountability.
Accumulating and counting wealth provides a close material expression of attachment to the immediate.
